brief:
Cartier is exploring the use of AI to improve client retention in its high jewellery division. The maison has observed that clients who purchase bespoke commissions — one-of-one pieces with price points typically exceeding €200,000 — often do not return for subsequent commissions despite expressing satisfaction with the original piece and ongoing relationship with their advisor. The client relations team believes the post-purchase relationship deteriorates after the six-month service follow-up, and that timely, personalised re-engagement could surface latent demand among dormant high-value clients.

Cartier's brand leadership has set constraints on any AI integration. The technology must remain invisible to the client; the perception of human craftsmanship, personal attention, and advisor-led relationships must be preserved entirely. The high jewellery division operates on objective scarcity — each piece is unique and cannot be replicated — and the client base in this segment overwhelmingly values discretion and privacy over peer recognition or social display. Advisors currently manage client relationships through personal knowledge and handwritten notes; any system that appears to replace this intimacy with algorithmic pattern-matching would be rejected by both advisors and clients.

The maison's innovation lab has been asked to evaluate whether AI could support the advisory relationship without surfacing to the client, and whether personalisation at the individual level is appropriate for a segment where exclusivity depends on the perception that each relationship is singular and unmechanised. Cartier's leadership is aware that competitors in the haute joaillerie space have not publicly adopted client-facing AI, and wishes to understand whether this absence reflects genuine unsuitability or merely market hesitancy.
